items.title: Timestral: Mistral's time-series foundation models
items.content:
Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.

Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.

Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.

Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.

Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.

Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.

Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.

We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.

TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.

fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.

Family of models optimised for every specification

Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.

Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its…

items.title: Updates to site guidelines and AI/LLM tags
items.content:
I've been having to perform an increasing number of moderation actions surrounding the vibecoding tag and AI/LLM related content. I started reading Lobsters because it had the most interesting viewpoints related to computing. During that time, I've found that this community is at it's best when it's trying to, in good faith, help others grow. In lieu of a larger and more rambling discussion on this point, we would like to try two changes encourage that behavior again and re-focus topicality around ensuring that content submitted to the site should, at a minimum, be respectful of a reader's time and intelligence.

The first adjustment is two updates to the about page, which try to provide a bit more clarity in what we consider topical and what constitutes self promotion:

Lobsters is a computing-focused community centered around discussing links. Our goal is to learn, craft, collaborate, and share interesting viewpoints.

The administrator is Peter Bhat Harkins ("pushcx"), contact him or another moderator with any support issues. Lobsters was launched on July 3rd, 2012 by joshua stein  (who is no longer running it, so please quit bugging him with site stuff) with careful design touches to encourage a healthy community:

At this risk of writing a mission statement, it seemed worth explaining what the site is and hopes to be to visitors from the first sentence of /about. (This original text came from an intro post .)

Topicality: Lobsters is focused pretty narrowly on computing; tags like art don't imply every piece of art is on-topic.  Some rules of thumb for great stories to submit: Will this improve the reader's next program? Will it deepen their understanding of their last program? Will it be more interesting in five or ten years? Is this compelling material that will seed a discussion, or is it just an artifact?

Pending an upcoming deploy, we no longer allow submissions which are code repositories. While, at first blush, this may seem odd for a community which is primarily centered around programming but it does eliminate the bulk of the "low effort, self promotional" submissions we've been seeing on the site. We've also found that being dropped into a new codebase doesn't start discussions because the reader has to have enough subject matter experience to immediately recognize what's novel or otherwise worth talking about. Instead, we are more interested in content around code bases which cover why it was created, the purpose it serves, the challenges overcome, and the reasons why it's a useful artifact in the ecosystem.

Some things that are off-topic here but popular on larger, similar sites: entrepreneurship; management; careers; news about companies that employ a lot of programmers; investing; world events; anthropology; self-help; personal productivity systems; last-resort customer service requests via public shaming; "I wanted to see what this site's amazing users think about this off-topic thing"; and defining the single morally correct economic and political system for the entire world when we can't even settle tabs vs. spaces.

We're listing "careers" as off-topic to try to head off posts about interviewing, promotions, burnout, and farming . We have the  job tag because it's nice to help people connect to jobs, but the topic of getting a good job, weaving jobs into a career over your lifetime, and work is a different thing than the actual programming itself.

Self-promotion: It's great to have authors participate in the community, but we do not want the community to be exploited as a write-only tool for product announcements or driving traffic to their work. As a rule of thumb, self-promotional activity should be less than a quarter of one's stories and comments in the last year. New users ( first 70 days ) are not allowed to submit self-promo.

items.title: Wine ported to OpenBSD
Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: AI Images Can Obscure the Reality of Factory Farms | Prompt revision steered AI-generated images towards idyllic scenes even when told to be realistic
items.content:
Researchers found a hidden feature steered the AI-generated images towards more idyllic scenes.

An estimated 99% of farm animals in the United States are raised in concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs . Often called factory farms, these facilities raise livestock in densely packed, enclosed spaces, with some housing tens of thousands of animals at one time.

Yet when Kehan (Sky) Sheng, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia, used generative AI to create animal-farming visuals for her presentations, she received idyllic scenes: cows roaming on pasture, pigs rooting in mud, red barns and windmills.

Sheng found an explanation deep within the technical documentation for DALL-E 3, OpenAI’s text-to-image AI model for ChatGPT: An internal language model rewrites or expands user prompts to add more details before images are generated.

“The moment that I found out it is actually a prompt revision that is erasing all the reality, I was absolutely shocked,” says Sheng. “That’s insane.”

In a new Technology in Society paper, Sheng and co-authors analyzed 4,800 independently generated images and found that ChatGPT defaulted to pastoral imagery when prompted to depict dairy and pig farms , even when they requested more realistic images. However, when researchers disabled the underlying prompt revision, the generated images depicted more intensive livestock farming.

The results reveal how efforts to put guardrails on generative AI models can have unintended consequences — and raise questions about how these models shape users’ perceptions of where our food comes from.

AI models are known to have inherited human societal biases and stereotypes , including perpetuating and normalizing violence against animals . These biases can enter through training data sources, which often reflect skewed representations of the world through stock images, advertisements, art and other human-created material, as well as human labeling and model design .

But the researchers identified another source of bias: ChatGPT’s automatic prompt revision process, in which an internal language model rewrites or adds details to a user’s instructions before passing them to DALL-E 3 for image generation. As of publication, users are not being notified of these revisions. Sentient reached out to OpenAI for comment but did not receive a response prior to publication.

In the study, the internal language model expanded basic prompts, such as “a dairy farm,” with pastoral details, including healthy cows grazing on lush green grass, before generating images. All images generated from the basic dairy-farm prompt depicted pastoral settings, as were 99% of those generated from the basic pig-farm prompt. This sharply contrasts with the reality of U.S. dairy production, where fewer than 3% of lactating cows are raised primarily on pasture , and pork production, where 87% of the industry’s building capacity is enclosed confinement with no outdoor access .

When authors instructed the model not to revise their prompts, the results shifted notably: 60% of requests for dairy-farm images depicted cows housed indoors and accessing feed through metal barriers, while 96% of pig-farm images showed pigs indoors behind metal railings on concrete floors.

Prompt revision helps AI companies create more detailed images by filling gaps in vague prompts — for example, “a pig farm” doesn’t specify the type, size or location of the farm — and helps models follow guidelines, such as removing public figures and harmful biases . But the function can backfire. In 2024, Google paused its AI-image generator after its Gemini model depicted the U.S. Founding Fathers and Nazi-era soldiers as Black .

This factory farm study offers another example of how efforts to steer AI outputs toward certain goals can have unintended consequences.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-112991 📢 Source: CIRCL 💣 CVSS Score: 6.3 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True The html_to_markdown expansion module in MISP Modules contains a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its is_safe_url() URL validation function. The BLOCKED_RANGES list used to reject unsafe destination addresses was incomplete, omitting several critical IP address ranges. Specifically, the following ranges were not blocked: 0.0.0.0/8 (unspecified, which routes to loopback on Linux), 100.64.0.0/10 (carrier-grade NAT per RFC 6598), ::/128 (IPv6 unspecified), fc00::/7 (IPv6 Unique Local Addresses), and fe80::/10 (IPv6 link-local). The existing list only covered IPv4 loopback (127.0.0.0/8), RFC 1918 private ranges, IPv4 link-local (169.254.0.0/16), and IPv6 loopback (::1/128). An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify MISP attributes that trigger the html_to_markdown expansion module could supply URLs pointing to these unblocked internal address ranges. Because the module fetches the URL server-side to convert HTML content to Markdown, the request is made from the MISP server's network context. This allows an attacker to probe and read responses from internal services, carrier-grade NAT infrastructure, or link-local endpoints that would otherwise be unreachable from external networks. IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms (e.g., [::ffff:0.0.0.0]) also bypassed the existing checks. The security impact is primarily confidentiality: an attacker can read data served by internal services reachable from the MISP server. The MISP instance itself is not compromised, but it is abused as a proxy to access otherwise restricted network resources. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-19T22:19:50.011Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112991

items.title: It's still ok to enjoy programming
items.content:
Reading Hacker News makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming .

Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious.

To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point.

I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like Agda . There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun [0] .

A few weekends ago: recursion schemes . Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas [1] . But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why entire papers get written about Monoids . Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding.

I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.

It's OK to enjoy things [2] . Doing so requires no economic justification.

Footnotes: [0] Take the time to understand Fin one day. It is beautiful.

[1] I'm not there yet, but the goal of studying this is to give myself another tool for reasoning about program correctness algebraically (a topic I cover in my book !)

[2] I also have a blast vibe-coding. I've got a suite of apps for which I've never looked at a line of code. I suspect doing so would horrify me. "Programming" this way is also fun. Often extremely so. But in its own unique way.

items.title: One Hash Bloom Filters
items.content:
Note: as always, all my public writing is written by hand by me.

A bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure that allows you to quickly and cheaply answer the question "is key X in this set?" with either "definitely not" or "probably" .

You pick a false positive rate that is acceptable for your workload and hardware, add keys to the set, and check for their existence later on.

Bloom filters use a small amount of memory compared to the cardinality of the set, and are computationally very cheap. For these reasons, they're frequently used in high performance data systems.

For example, a database might keep an in-memory bloom filter and check it before actually going to disk when looking up rows. This saves substantial amounts of very slow disk IO.

We also use them all over the place in the Bluesky backend. They allow us to save millions of queries per second against our Scylla database when looking up blocks, mutes, labels, and more. For instance, we can often answer the question "does user X block user Y" without even hitting the database.

Here's the last several days of some of our bloom filter positive hit rates:

The above yellow line has a roughly 1% positive rate, which means that 99% of the time, we can completely skip querying our database. This has been critical in our ability to scale the site and operate the site cheaply.

A bloom filter is an array of bits and k hash functions. You choose the size of the array and k before hand, and want to right-size it to your workload to achieve a specific false positive rate.

To add a key to the set, run it through the k hash functions and set the bits at each of those locations.

To check if a a key is in the set, hash it k times and check each resulting location in the bit array. If any bits are zero, the key was never added. If all bits are set to one, it might be in the set.

Here's an example of a potential positive:

While much cheaper than going to disk, computing k independent hashes per key is still a bit expensive for very high performance systems.

In 2008, Kirsch and Mitzenmacher wrote a paper demonstrating that two hashes can get you the same output. The math is far over my head, but if you derive the i -th location as (hash_1 + i*hash_2) % n , then the false positive rate is effectively the same as using k independent hashes. Phew!

bits-and-blooms/bloom maintained by Daniel Lemire (a huge inspiration of mine, you should buy his book ) is a fantastic double hash bloom filter implementation written in go. It runs 128-bit murmur3 twice to get four 64-bit values, then combines them to produce all k bit locations. We used this in production at Bluesky for a long time.

For the Bluesky backend, we essentially do a SELECT * FROM blocks , mutes, list items, etc. every time one the processes starts, and add all the items to the bloom filter. There's also a real time atproto firehose consumer inserting items in to bloom filters (even during process startup), so there is a race condition if you're not careful.

The problem with the bits-and-blooms library is that it's not internally thread-safe, so we needed to wrap all bloom filter access in a mutex lest we suffer a data race. pprof showed that mutex contention was actually the bottleneck in launching the process. A single deploy used to take 90 minutes to roll out fully because of this!

So my colleague Jasmine forked the library and created atomic-bloom , which uses atomic CPU instructions to do the same logic, but safely and without mutexes. This led to substantially less contention and was massively faster than the mutex-based approach. Our deploys dropped from 90 minutes to about 15, which enabled us to ship faster and with greater confidence. Awesome!

For Bluesky, the answer is no . Contention was our original problem, not the number of hash functions or other factors, thus by Amdahl's Law we did not receive any further speedup resulting in a noticeable impact. However, it's still fun to go deeper and…

items.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan and back
items.content:
Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey’s length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky.

The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock.

“We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we’re twice as high as air traffic and we’re above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen , founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we’re still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.”

There have been many past technology demonstrations and attempts to make stratospheric platforms commercially viable since the late 1990s, Frandsen said. In Sceye’s case, the company began testing a series of smaller prototypes in 2016 before eventually reaching the stratosphere with a 215-foot (65-meter) length version in 2021. The latest version extends to 270 feet (83 meters).

The lighter-than-air platform has also benefited from advances in material sciences that “were either not discovered or not understood back in the late 1990s,” Frandsen said. He highlighted the example of the discovery of graphene in 2004, which “greatly helped us optimize strength relative to weight on our hull, the energy density of our batteries, and performance relative to the area and weight of our solar panels.”

The design could eventually scale up to a high altitude platform system (HAPS) capable of lifting payloads as heavy as 551 pounds (250 kilograms). That would be between 25 and 50 times more payload capacity than competing stratospheric platforms like high-flying drones, according to Helena , a US nonprofit organization with a for-profit investment arm that has invested in Sceye.

Sceye’s current platform has already done multiple flight demonstrations with payloads exceeding 220 pounds (100 kilograms) and can provide up to 1 kilowatt of onboard power capability for any devices that it may be carrying.

A heavier payload and higher power capacity opens the door to bigger mission possibilities, such as someday using a single Sceye platform hovering in the stratosphere to provide mobile broadband coverage equivalent to 500 ground-based cell towers. That may prove useful for both enhancing commercial telecommunications services and providing emergency coverage during disaster scenarios.

Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen from inside its hangar after launching from New Mexico on August 9, 2026.

Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen from inside its hangar after launching from New Mexico on August 9, 2026.

The concept was put to the test after Sceye’s platform launched from its New Mexico base on August 9, 2026, and traveled more than 9,320 miles (15,000 kilometers) across the Pacific to reach Japan. That 13-day journey required the airship to navigate through strong winds and avoid potential bad weather “during a window of typhoon season,” said Johnny Truong , chief technology officer of Sceye.

items.title: A5 is a geospatial index that partitions the world into pentagonal cells. The cells are available at 31 resolution levels, from a handful covering the whole world down to less than 30mm²
items.content:
A5 is a geospatial index that partitions the world into pentagonal cells . The cells are available at 31 resolution levels , from a handful covering the whole world down to less than 30mm², and every cell at a given resolution has exactly the same area . Each cell is identified by a 64-bit integer, which is frozen from v1.0: an A5 cell ID stored today will refer to the same place in the future.

Once data is in cells, very different datasets can be joined, aggregated and compared directly: points can be counted per cell, as with the density of holiday rentals across a city, and regions such as countries or parcels of land become coverings , sets of cells which support union, intersection and difference.

Equal area, single topology : every cell is an exactly equal-area pentagon with 5 neighbors, so aggregates are free of bias from unequal cell sizes. See A5 vs H3 .

Built for big data : cell IDs follow a space-filling curve that never crosses itself, so polygons and coverings are compact ID ranges. Billions of cells can be filled, combined and counted in seconds.

Fast & rich API : high-level functions for indexing , hierarchy , traversal and coverings , with a native Rust core.

Strong ecosystem : official libraries for TypeScript , Python and Rust , with DuckDB , PostgreSQL , R, QGIS and deck.gl integrations. See the Ecosystem .

Quickstart : index your first cell in your language of choice

DuckDB playground : use DuckDB to experiment with A5

Examples : interactive examples showcasing the system

API Reference : every function, with snippets in each language

items.title: A5 v1.0
items.content:
It has been 18 months since the first announcement of A5. What started off as an experiment in visualization (and an obsession with pentagons) has grown into a useful tool, with a wealth of libraries, tools and software building on top.

Today I'm excited to announce that the v1.0 version of A5 is out, bringing a powerful set of features and performance improvements as well as crystallizing the grid and index definition for the future.

If you're new to A5, in a nutshell it is a grid system that allows the representation of any position, line or polygon region on the globe as a pentagonal cell (or collection of cells), each represented as a compact 64-bit integer.

The industry term for this is a Discrete Global Grid System (DGGS), and there are already a number of other systems out there which are powering some of the world's largest companies and data analytics pipelines.

For a concrete example of an application leveraging A5, take a look at the FIRMS Explorer which uses A5 to aggregate 631 million fire detections worldwide since 2000.

With v1.0 we are committing to keeping the grid layout and the cell IDs frozen going forward. While the system will evolve and grow, for example by adding more utility functions, the fundamentals will stay fixed so applications, databases and workflows will be able to rely on an A5 cell representing a specific geographic location into the future.

The community around the project has grown, in particular with the DuckDB and R implementations, whose beautiful sites arguably even put the official A5 site to shame! As such, going forward, the documentation on the A5 website will present code snippets and API documentation in these languages, as well as the officially supported TypeScript, Rust and Python libraries.

New in v1.0 is a whole new set of functions for working with collections of cells, known as coverings .

When working with coverings, you can now use set operations: union , intersect and difference , predicates: contains and overlaps and measuring functions: count and area .

By using compacted data and these operations, it is possible to process billions of cells efficiently without having to uncompact the data, as was necessary before. An example workflow might be to union several coverings from database queries, intersect with a polygon or spherical cap and then filter a collection of points against the resulting covering. See the example workflow .

Geometrically, it is impossible to split an A5 pentagon into more pentagons in such a manner that the result exactly overlaps; the same is true of hexagons - unlike quadrilaterals and triangles, which can be split exactly. The A5 hierarchy is thus logical, and only approximately spatial.

In order to support resampling and other operations, a new function cellToSubcells has been added. While this is slower than the cellToChildren API, it produces a correct covering (by centroid) of the cell. The inverse, cellToSupercell , is also available.

One of the key strengths of A5 has always been the guarantee that every cell is exactly the same area at a given resolution, which means that any analysis run using the system is free of bias due to unequal cell sizes. New in v1.0 , all the cells at all resolutions have the same pentagonal topology. This is in contrast to hexagonal DGGSs, which must include 12 pentagonal cells that complicate the topology and break the pure equal-area guarantee.

One of the important characteristics of a grid system is its support across a range of tools and software, both in industry and academia. By standardizing on a definition of the grid and cell identifiers, it is easy to move data between systems and applications. For example, the FIRMS Explorer above was built using:

Geoparquet.io to aggregate the data: gpio add a5 input.parquet output.parquet --resolution 5

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: The RTX 5090 now costs EUR 1,830 more than it did a month ago
items.content:
Most of the increase happened before the story broke. The median rose steadily through late September and early October, and only a small part of the 31 % came after the reports.

Each day: every retailer listing's last in-stock scrape, EUR, EU retailers (Webhallen and Morele excluded). A card's price is its cheapest listing. Cards in stock change daily, so day-to-day moves partly reflect which cards were available. Not a forecast. The cheapest single listing tells a similar story, with one jump. It sat around €5,280 for most of early October, went up to about €7,350 on 17 and 18 October, and fell back to roughly €6,900 on the 19th.

Availability got thinner too. At the peak, 10 stores had a 5090 in stock. In the last few days it has been 4 to 6.

The rise is not new. We follow a fixed basket of 11 RTX 5090 models that were in stock in at least 80% of weeks since late May. Their average price is up about 84 % from the week of 25 May to the week of 12 October. The last week alone was roughly + 10 %.

The climb has been fairly steady since July and sped up in September. So the last 30 days are the steep part of a longer trend.

Fixed basket of 11 RTX 5090 models in stock in at least 80% of weeks. Index of the basket's average cheapest price, 25 May = 100. EU retailers, EUR. What this does and doesn't show

The timing of the reports does not show a cause. Prices were rising before them, and other things were going on at the same time that we can't separate out.

Reports, not an announcement. The discontinuation is unconfirmed, and Nvidia has denied it.

Day-to-day moves are noisy. Which cards are in stock changes daily, so a single day can jump because the mix changed. The trend is more reliable than any one day.

EU only. We leave out Webhallen (Sweden) and Morele (Poland) because they price in other currencies. This may not match the US or other regions.

Not a forecast. We don't know where prices go from here.

Every day we take each retailer listing's last in-stock price, in EUR. A card's price is its cheapest in-stock listing. The headline number is the median of those card prices across all models in stock that day.

Listings with the same EAN are merged into one card. Obvious outliers, prices under half or over three times a card's usual price, are dropped. The weekly basket only counts cards with at least 3 valid days in a week, and weeks with fewer than 5 days of data are skipped.

Biomedical Magazine Feature October 2026

Tech to Replace Animal Testing Is Almost Ready. Scientists Are Not

Changing habits may be the hardest engineering challenge of all

Lab rats have long been a mainstay of biomedical research and drug development. N ow, technologies such as Emulate’s Lung-on-a-Chip aim to model human biology without relying on animals.

Seventeen years ago, cell biologist Donald Ingber and his colleagues at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering submitted a paper to the journal Science describing their model human lung. It was smaller than a USB stick and made of a clear polymer slab containing narrow channels, which were lined with the type of cells that line a lung’s air sacs and blood vessels. When air was pumped through hollow chambers beside the channels, the device rhythmically expanded and contracted—it “breathed.”

This lifelike movement was a dramatic change from previous generations of lung models, which typically used static cultures of lung tissue that were unable to simulate the movements essential to lung function. When exposed to inflammatory proteins and bacteria , Ingber’s artificial lung reacted much as living lungs would. And exposure to silica nanoparticles used to model the effects of ultrafine particulates revealed that movement affected how tissues absorbed them.

Donald Ingber led the team that developed the first human lung-on-a-chip at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute. Sam Ogden

It was a powerful proof-of-principle demonstration of a system that could be used to test drugs and other chemicals, providing a complement and even an alternative to testing in tissue cultures or in animals . Even so, the editors at Science were hesitant. They rejected the paper and suggested that Ingber’s team also run the tests in mice.

It wasn’t an unreasonable request: Harvard’s lung system was new and comparing the results it generated to results from mice would help validate it. Ingber’s team ran the suggested experiments and resubmitted their study a year later, in 2010, at which point it was published . (It has since been cited by nearly 5,400 other papers.) Still, the incident spoke to how animal models have been the default of modern biomedical research.

An early lung-on-a-chip developed at Harvard’s Wyss Institute used microfluidic channels lined with human cells to reproduce key features of lung function. Wyss Institute at Harvard University

A recent story told by Ilka Maschmeyer , a translational toxicology researcher and executive at the German biotech company TissUse , shows how much things have changed. TissUse specializes in building organ-on-a-chip systems —the conversational name for systems like Ingber’s lung—that are used by pharmaceutical companies for research. A few months ago, says Maschmeyer, a pharmaceutical company approached TissUse after being denied permission by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to run a clinical trial of a new drug. The problem: It had presented animal data, but the FDA wanted data from organs-on-a-chip or some comparable alternative. The standards had come full circle.

The lung chip re -creates the interface between an air sac and a blood vessel, with human lung and endothelial cells growing on opposite sides of a porous membrane. Vacuum channels rhythmically stretch and relax the tissue to mimic breathing, reproducing mechanical forces that can affect how lung cells respond to substances they encounter. In one experiment, researchers added bacteria to the air channel and white blood cells to the blood channel; the immune cells crossed the membrane and engulfed the bacteria, reproducing an inflammatory response.

The moment spoke to a trend, perhaps even the early days of a fundamental shift, away from the use of animals in toxicology and drug development. “It’s rare still,” says Maschmeyer, “but I think it’s going to be more and more frequent.”

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Linux kernel 7.3 has been released
items.content:
Linux 7.3 changelog. Summary: Linux 7.3 improves gaming performance on low-end GPUs by improving VRAM management; it also adds completed support for assigning individual BPF task schedulers for each individual cgroup and more performant cgroup scheduling; better btrfs and ext4 performance; support for a new sandboxing technique using a new failfs pseudofilesystem + a new fchroot(2) system call; support for the RWF_DONTCACHE flag when opening block devices as an alternative to Direct I/O; a more powerful binfmt_misc for distros like NixOS, SMB server support for Apple Time Machine extensions and other improvements; userfaultfd(2) support for better tracking the working set of VM guest memory; and better performance for FUSE servers using io_uring . As always, there are many other features, new drivers, improvements and fixes. You might also be interested in the list of changes done by Linux Weekly News: part 1 , part 2 차례

Improved VRAM management for low-end GPUs

Support for cgroup sub-schedulers (sched_ext) has been completed

Improved cgroup scheduling and other task scheduling improvements

New sandboxing technique with failfs + fchroot(2)

More powerful binfmt_misc for sophisticated distros

SMB server support for Apple Time Machine extensions

Better separation between kernel threads and PID 1

Add support userfaultfd: working set tracking for VM guest memory

RWF_DONTCACHE for block devices, an alternative for Direct I/O

Tablets, touch screens, keyboards, mouses

Voltage, current regulators, power capping, power supply

1.1. Improved VRAM management for low-end GPUs

When your GPU does not have (as it's usually the case) enough VRAM (Video RAM), different applications can end up competing for VRAM. Due to the way VRAM allocation worked, if two applications consumed a lot of VRAM, the one that arrived the latest, which could have more priority, could not get enough VRAM and end up allocation space from the GTT (system RAM accessible by the GPU). This release allows using the dmem cgroup to alleviate the situation: Instead of backing off immediately, the system will try evicting unprotected buffers from the domain to make space for the protected one. This ensures that applications can actually use all the memory protection awarded to them by the system, without being prone to ping-ponging. Recommended read: Fixing AMDGPU's VRAM management for low-end GPUs Cover letter: cgroup/dmem,drm/ttm: Improve protection in contended cases

1.2. Support for cgroup sub-schedulers (sched_ext) has been completed

After some work, this release has finally completed the implementation of sched_ext : this allows a cgroup have its processes be managed by its own BPF-based task scheduler. Different cgroups can have different BPF sub-schedulers and take different scheduling decisions. Recommended LWN article: Sched-ext: enqueue() for sub-schedulers and proxy-execution support Documentation: Extensible Scheduler Class Merge commit: Pull sched_ext updates

1.3. Improved cgroup scheduling and other task scheduling improvements

Cgroup scheduling has always been problematic and painful. Fair/cgroup isn't working for a number of people; typically the complaint is latencies and/or overhead. The problems starts with weight distribution and end with hierachical picks. This release improves cgroup scheduling in these fronts: It adds various cgroup weight distribution methods via cgroup_mode: 'up', 'max', 'concur' and 'tasks' - with the default being 'concur' which is the most precise (yet also most expensive version). Finally, change cgroup scheduling to a single runqueue. This release also improves the scheduling latency of tasks with shorter slice duration by mainly canceling, updating or minimizing the protection of the running tasks when appropriate. And cluster scheduling in the presence of asymmetric capacity has been fixed. Merge commit: Pull scheduler updates

items.title: Google’s AI pinned another man’s sex crime on a doctor, and a German court says Google must answer for it
items.content:
The Google logo. Image: Google LLC / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain (trademark), cropped

Google’s AI search told users that an Aachen doctor had been convicted of a sex crime. The conviction belonged to a different man, and on September 24 the Aachen Regional Court banned Google from repeating it , ruling that the company answers for what its AI Mode says. It is the second German court this year to treat Google’s AI answers as Google’s own words, and the first ruling to say so has now been settled rather than tested on appeal.

The man who went to court is a professor and former head of a neuroradiology clinic. According to the court’s order, Google’s AI Mode answered searches about him with a detailed story: that he had been suspended in February 2024 over an accusation from his secretary, convicted of sexual coercion in March 2026 with a suspended sentence, and paid off in a six-figure labour court settlement. The court accepted his sworn statement that every part of it concerned another former university professor, and added that it knew this itself, because the criminal case it was citing had been brought against someone else.

The doctor asked Google to delete the text on August 28 and followed up with a formal legal warning on September 15. Neither worked. The court’s 8th civil chamber then acted without hearing Google first, citing the urgency of false claims that were “publicly visible” to an unlimited audience. Google Ireland, which runs Google Search in the EU, now faces a fine of up to €250,000 for each breach, or detention of its managers, if it repeats three versions of the text. Google can still challenge the order.

The court’s reasoning is blunt: Google “provides AI-generated search and is therefore also responsible for the answers generated in this context.” It added that checking would have been easy: had Google “confronted its own AI” with the doctor’s objections, it would have found the statements were false.

That reasoning comes almost word for word from Munich. On May 28 the Munich Regional Court I ruled (case 26 O 869/26) on AI Overviews that told searchers two Munich publishing companies were “known for dubious business practices”, ran subscription traps and kept changing their names to avoid being traced. None of the linked sources said that; the first one cited did not mention the companies at all.

Google argued that it was only summarising other people’s pages, the same defence that has long protected search engines in Germany. The court disagreed. AI Overviews, it said, do not just show links but make “independent, new and substantive statements” built by evaluating and combining third-party sites, so Google must treat them as its own, including as the provider of an AI system under the EU’s AI Act. “Only it has influence over the AI,” the judges wrote.

Google said at the time it would appeal. That appeal has ended in a settlement, The Decoder reported on Saturday; the terms are not known and neither Google nor the publishers would comment. The upshot is that no higher court has ruled, so the Munich judgment is not binding precedent, but lower courts such as Aachen are already following it.

Not every German court agrees. In June the Berlin Regional Court II threw out a trademark claim by the perfume company Coty over AI Overviews and AI Mode answers listing “scent twins” of its brands, finding that users see the features as an extended form of search results summarising other people’s content. Google’s lawyer in that case said :

The Berlin Regional Court confirms that, despite the use of AI, Google remains a neutral intermediary and does not become a provider of its own content.

The Berlin case was about trademarks rather than false claims about people, and the Munich and Aachen judges did not have to deal with it. But the split shows the question is far from settled in Germany’s courts.

most negative number has no corresponding positive number. For example, with

signed 8-bit numbers, the most negative number is -128 , whilst the most

positive number is 127 . This quirk shows up in various cases, but for the

purpose of this post, I am concerned with signed integer division, where x/-1

mathematically should produce -x , but in the case where x is the most

negative number, that is not possible. For 32-bit integers, which I arbitrarily

decide are the most common, this means that one out of every 2⁶⁴ possible inputs

is impossible to represent correctly - leading to the somewhat clickbaity title

of this post, and some recently fixed troubles in the Futhark compiler. In this

post I will explain what the actual problem is for a language implementation,

how we fix it, and what the performance cost looks like. The main audience of

this post is other language implementers, but I think the concepts involved are

simple enough that anyone curious about low level issues can follow along.

The Futhark compiler has multiple backends, but the most important ones work by

generating C code. This has many practical advantages:

It is easy to debug the generated code because it is easy to read and modify

Most systems have a C compiler (or easy access to one), meaning Futhark has

fewer dependencies, is portable, and doesn’t need to bundle native code

Many languages can interoperate with C, so by exposing Futhark as a C API,

That said, there are also disadvantages:

Some code patterns are hard to express (or express efficiently) in C. This is

mainly the case for advanced language features such as coroutines, tail

calls, or garbage collection. Fortunately Futhark is pretty boring from a

It is very easy to accidentally generate C code that is subtly wrong. This

C is of course renowned as a very safe and easy-to-use language, because C

programmers never make coding mistakes. The few times they do make mistakes, it

is often due to mishandling of pointers or array sizes, leading to buffer

overflows, heap smashing, etc. These are actually not the main problem with

generating C from Futhark, as Futhark itself is memory-safe, and systematically

inserting in bounds checks in generated code is easy ( although a little more

No, the main problem we’ve had is actually undefined behaviour. As is by now

well-known, C specifies various events as explicitly undefined, meaning not only

that a C compiler can assume it will never occur, but also that no particular

result is guaranteed should a program perform one of the undefined operations.

Some causes of undefined behaviour are obvious and easy to avoid: reading arrays

out-of-bounds, using freed memory, etc. But C has a long list of more obscure

cases. My favourite example is that in C99, it is undefined behaviour if a

source code file does not end with a final newline character. Yet we have

honestly not spent that much time dealing with that particular issue in Futhark.

No, the main problem, and now we are finally returning to the premise in the

post, is that signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour in C. This is

particularly insidious since most programmers have a mental model of fixed-size

integer arithmetic where overflow is a natural event, and so does the actual

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: The US is ordering every civilian agency to rip out DeepSeek, even tools built on it
items.content:
Markwayne Mullin in his official US Senate portrait, taken before he became Homeland Security Secretary. Image: United States Senate / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain, cropped

The US government has ordered every federal civilian agency to strip DeepSeek out of its computers and stop buying it, along with any third-party product built on the Chinese lab's AI. The Department of Homeland Security filed notice of the order with the Federal Register on Monday, under a 2018 supply chain law that lets it bar risky technology from government systems.

The order, numbered 2026-01 and signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, is dated July 24, 2026. It was kept out of public view until this week. Its notice is due to appear in the Federal Register on Tuesday, October 20, under docket DHS-2026-0628.

The order tells all civilian agencies to do two things. First, exclude Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence, its affiliates and their products from purchasing "effective immediately", including agency-approved product lists, e-commerce marketplaces and similar buying channels. Second, remove products from DeepSeek and its affiliates, "and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations", from agency IT systems immediately.

That second clause is the wide one. DeepSeek's models are released as open weights, so they turn up inside other companies' tools as well as in DeepSeek's own app and website. The order does not list which products it means, and it does not say how agencies should treat a DeepSeek model running on a US company's servers. It also comes days after DeepSeek updated its cheap Flash model , which it says now beats Claude Opus 5 at some coding tasks.

It does not reach the military or spy agencies. The order applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies "except for their national security systems and secure compartmented information systems", which fall under the Pentagon and the Director of National Intelligence.

The order's summary of risks says DeepSeek's servers are in China and that Chinese law "permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure". It says DeepSeek's sign-up process collects personal information and may "track and digitally fingerprint users", and that its apps work by having people type in information, which could mean sensitive data from US government staff or contractors ends up in China.

Combined with public data, that information "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs", the order says. It adds that the models "may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities", and cites a February 2025 NowSecure audit that found multiple critical flaws in DeepSeek's iPhone app.

The order's evidence is drawn from public material: DeepSeek's own privacy policy, a 2020 DHS business advisory on Chinese data risks and an April 2025 House Select Committee on China report. It doesn't describe any case of government data reaching DeepSeek.

Agencies that can't comply can ask for an exception, such as having the order not apply to them, to certain actions, or a delay. Requests must be made in writing within 60 days of the order's issue, with a "compelling justification", for example the impact on mission-critical work, and any alternative safeguards. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reviews them and approves or refuses in writing.

Until DeepSeek products are gone, agencies are told to monitor traffic in and out of their networks, step up logging, add controls against data leaving their systems and flag anything unusual. CISA can help agencies that lack the skills to comply, and the Secretary must review the order within a year and every year after.

items.title: Fudan University researchers found ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok and Google AI cited a made-up concept within seven days. Placement on frequently cited sites produced earlier citations than volume.
items.content:
ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Google AI each cited posts about a made-up concept within seven days of the posts going up, according to a paper from researchers at Fudan University.

The researchers published the posts from ordinary accounts on nine sites the tested tools already cited often. On two other topics, an opinion question with existing discussion and a made-up product, the same four tools picked up little in the same seven days.

The paper uses the label “Google AI” and links to Google’s general AI site, but it doesn’t specify which Google product was tested. The tests were conducted in March and April, and the paper was posted on arXiv on Oct. 8.

In March, the Fudan team ran 120 questions through 10 AI search tools and recorded the sites each tool cited. The researchers classify ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Google AI as English-web tools; the other six, including Doubao and DeepSeek, are Chinese-web tools.

Across those questions, Reddit was the most-cited site for Google AI and Grok, YouTube for Perplexity, and Wikipedia for ChatGPT. Six to 10 of each tool’s 10 most-cited sites accepted posts from ordinary users.

In April tests of 22 posting platforms, the researchers rated Medium, GitHub, LinkedIn, and Facebook easy to join and post on, while Reddit’s karma requirements and strict deletions made posting harder.

For each tool, the team then picked its most-cited site that a new account could post on, which gave them nine sites, including Medium, YouTube, and Sohu.

The research team posted articles about the fictional “Cactus Gravity Protocol,” whether AI would supplant junior programmers inside of five years, and a fictional keyboard. The first drafts of each article were created using ChatGPT, then each was manually revised and carried planted details (e.g., fabricated names and numbers) to allow the authors to identify if the AI tools repeated that information.

The researchers ran checks before posting to verify that none of the tools provided an informative response to either of the fictional topics or repeated the planted information. Following posting, the researchers ran the same five questions for each of the three topics on all tools daily for one week.

In June I covered a Cornell Tech paper on planted text that tested open-source research agents in a simulation. This team posted on the live web and queried the tools through their public interfaces.

Eight of the 10 tools cited the made-up concept, the Cactus Gravity Protocol, within a week, including all four English-web tools. Counting answers from the first day each tool cited the posts through the seventh day after posting, Grok linked to a post in 30 of 32 answers, Google AI in 15 of 33, Perplexity in 13 of 35, and ChatGPT in 7 of 20.

Fewer responses to questions included a planted detail from the source posts. Of Grok’s responses (n = 32), 53% did; for ChatGPT (n = 20), 10%; for Google AI (n = 33), 6%, and Perplexity (n = 35) none. In total, among all 10 tools and all three topics, there were links from 176 of the 1,004 answers to the posts during the week.

The only English-web tool that cited an “opinion” post was Perplexity, in 11.4% of its responses (n = 35), and none of the four cited keyboard posts within the week. The authors do not isolate which of the topic, competition, and type of question caused the differences across the three topics, since all three changed together.

In a follow-up, the team put one post each on Sohu, YouTube, and CSDN for 10 more made-up topics. Nine drew at least one citation or planted detail across the 10 tools, and Perplexity was one of the three tools that cited the most of them. The paper doesn’t break out the other English-web tools there.

items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.
